seed-claude-code-intro.title: Introducing Claude Code: a 4-minute first look
seed-claude-code-intro.hook: Four minutes that show you what an AI coding agent actually does, so the rest of the program makes sense.
seed-claude-code-intro.summary:
This short launch video from Anthropic shows Claude Code working inside a terminal. Instead of chatting in a browser and copying code back and forth, you describe what you want in plain language and the agent reads the project, proposes changes to files, runs commands and reports back.

You do not need to understand every line on screen. Watch for the shape of the loop: a person asks for something, the agent explores and plans, it asks permission before changing things, and the person reviews the result. That loop is the core skill you will practise for the next 66 days.

The video was made for an earlier release, so the interface you install today may look a little different. The idea has not changed.
takeaways: Claude Code is an agent: it can read files, edit them and run commands, not just answer questions.
You talk to it in plain language; being clear about the goal matters more than knowing syntax.
It asks for permission before acting, and you stay in charge of what gets accepted.
Your job shifts from typing code to describing, reviewing and testing.

steps.title: Watch the whole video once
steps.detail: Just watch. Do not take notes yet; get a feel for how the conversation with the agent flows.

steps.title: Watch again and pause at each request
steps.detail: Each time the person types a request, pause and say out loud what they asked for and what the agent did in response.

steps.title: Spot the permission moments
steps.detail: Notice when the agent stops to ask before editing a file or running a command. This is your safety net later.

steps.title: Write down three things you want to build
steps.detail: Small and concrete: a page about your hobby, a tool that tracks your water intake, a short animated title for a video.

exercise.title: My first three agent requests
exercise.goal: Turn vague ideas into clear requests you could give an agent tomorrow.
instructions: Pick three small things you would like to exist (a web page, a tiny tool, a short video).
For each one, write a request of 3–5 sentences: what it is, who it is for, what it should look like, and how you will know it works.
Under each request, write one question you think the agent might ask you back.
Paste all three into your journal for today.

quiz.q: What makes Claude Code different from a regular chatbot?
options: It can read and edit files and run commands in your project
It writes code but cannot explain it
It replaces the need to review anything
quiz.explain: An agent acts inside your project: it reads, edits and runs things, with your permission.

quiz.q: What is your main job when working with a coding agent?
options: Typing every line of code yourself
Describing the goal clearly and reviewing what it does
quiz.explain: Clear goals plus careful review is the core loop of this program.

quiz.q: Why does the agent ask for permission before some actions?
options: So you stay in control of changes to your files and system
To slow you down on purpose
quiz.explain: Permission prompts let you check edits and commands before they happen.

seed-mastering-claude-code.title: Mastering Claude Code in 30 minutes
seed-mastering-claude-code.hook: A talk from the team behind Claude Code on how they actually use it day to day.
seed-mastering-claude-code.summary:
This is a talk from Anthropic about getting real work done with Claude Code. It covers setting it up, giving it the right context, and the everyday habits that separate frustrating sessions from productive ones.

Some parts assume you already write code, so do not worry if a few examples go over your head. Focus on the habits: asking the agent questions about a project before changing it, asking it to make a plan first, keeping project notes in a CLAUDE.md file so it remembers your preferences, and stopping it early when it heads in the wrong direction.

Features and shortcuts change between versions. If something in the talk does not match your screen, check the current Claude Code docs; the working habits are what you are here for.
takeaways: Start by asking the agent to explain the project before you ask it to change anything.
Ask for a plan first, read it, then let it build. Planning saves time on anything bigger than a one-line fix.
A CLAUDE.md file in your project is a place for standing instructions the agent reads every session.
Interrupt early when it goes off track; redirecting is cheaper than undoing.
Give it a way to check its own work, such as running the app or a test.

steps.title: Watch with a notes file open
steps.detail: Every time a habit or tip is mentioned, write one line about it in your own words.

steps.title: Circle three habits you can use this week
steps.detail: Pick the ones that make sense for a beginner: explain-first, plan-first, and CLAUDE.md are good candidates.

steps.title: Create a practice folder
steps.detail: Make an empty folder, open a terminal in it, and start Claude Code there.

steps.title: Try explain, then plan, then build
steps.detail: Ask Claude to create a one-page website about a topic you love, but first tell it: 'Make a plan and wait for my OK before writing files.' Read the plan, adjust it, then approve.

steps.title: Ask it to write a CLAUDE.md
steps.detail: Tell it your preferences (for example: explain changes in simple words, keep things in plain HTML) and ask it to save them in CLAUDE.md.

exercise.title: Plan first, then build
exercise.goal: Experience the plan-then-build loop and leave a CLAUDE.md behind for future sessions.
instructions: In a new folder, start Claude Code and ask for a plan for a single-page site about something you care about. Ask it not to write files yet.
Reply with at least one change to the plan (a section to add, a colour, a tone).
Approve the plan and let it build. Open the page in your browser.
Ask Claude to create a CLAUDE.md with three preferences you want it to follow from now on.
Paste the final plan and your CLAUDE.md contents into your journal.

quiz.q: Before asking the agent to change an unfamiliar project, what is a good first move?
options: Ask it to explain how the project is organised
Delete files you do not understand
quiz.explain: Understanding first leads to better requests and fewer surprises.

quiz.q: What is CLAUDE.md used for?
options: A log of every command ever run
Standing instructions and project notes the agent reads each session
quiz.explain: It is a memory file for preferences, commands and conventions.

quiz.q: The agent starts doing something you did not want. What should you do?
options: Interrupt it and redirect with a clearer instruction
Wait until it finishes, then delete everything
quiz.explain: Stopping early and correcting course is much cheaper than undoing later.

quiz.q: Why ask for a plan before code on a bigger task?
options: It makes the agent faster at typing
You can catch misunderstandings before any files change
quiz.explain: Reading a plan is the cheapest moment to fix a wrong assumption.

suggestedDays.reason: Right after your first install: learn good habits before bad ones form.

seed-karpathy-intro-llm.title: Intro to Large Language Models (Andrej Karpathy, 1 hour)
seed-karpathy-intro-llm.hook: The clearest one-hour explanation of what is inside ChatGPT and Claude, from someone who helped build them.
seed-karpathy-intro-llm.summary:
Andrej Karpathy explains large language models for a general audience. He starts from the fact that a model is essentially a big file of learned numbers plus a small program to run it, then explains how that file is made: first by training on a huge amount of internet text to predict the next word, then by fine-tuning on example conversations so it behaves like a helpful assistant.

The second part looks at where things are heading: models that use tools like a browser or calculator, that work with images and audio, and the idea of the LLM as the core of a new kind of operating system. The final part covers security problems such as jailbreaks and prompt injection.

You do not need maths for this. If you only have time for part of it today, watch the first half (how models are trained and why they sometimes make things up) and come back to the rest.
takeaways: A language model is trained to predict the next piece of text; everything else grows out of that.
Pre-training on lots of text gives knowledge; fine-tuning on conversations turns it into an assistant.
Models can confidently produce wrong answers, so checking their output is part of the job.
Models get far more useful when they can use tools, which is exactly what coding agents do.
Prompt injection and jailbreaks are real risks whenever a model reads untrusted text.

steps.title: Watch the first half with notes
steps.detail: Write down, in your own words, the two training stages and what each one adds.

steps.title: Explain it to someone in two minutes
steps.detail: Out loud or in writing, explain to a friend how a model learns. If you get stuck, rewatch that part.

steps.title: Test the next-word idea yourself
steps.detail: Ask an AI assistant to continue an unfinished sentence in three different ways and notice how it picks likely continuations.

steps.title: Catch a confident mistake
steps.detail: Ask an assistant about a very obscure local fact you know well. Note whether it admits uncertainty or invents details.

steps.title: Skim the security section
steps.detail: Watch the last part on jailbreaks and prompt injection; note one example you understood.

exercise.title: My one-page LLM explainer
exercise.goal: Prove to yourself you understand the basics by explaining them simply.
instructions: Write a short explainer (150–250 words) titled 'How an AI model learns', aimed at a curious 12-year-old.
Cover: next-word prediction, the two training stages, and why the model can be wrong.
Add one real example from your own test where an assistant was wrong or unsure.
Save it in your journal. You will reuse it on your first web page later.

quiz.q: At its core, what is a large language model trained to do?
options: Store a copy of every website
Predict the next piece of text
quiz.explain: Next-token prediction is the base task everything else builds on.

quiz.q: What does fine-tuning on example conversations add?
options: More general knowledge from the web
quiz.explain: Pre-training gives knowledge; fine-tuning shapes it into a helpful assistant.

quiz.q: Why should you double-check an LLM's factual answers?
options: You should not; it is always correct
Because it can produce fluent, confident text that is wrong
quiz.explain: Fluent does not mean true; models can make things up.

quiz.q: What is prompt injection?
options: Hidden instructions in content the model reads that try to hijack its behaviour
A way to speed up training
quiz.explain: Untrusted text can contain instructions the model might follow.

seed-3b1b-gpt.title: But what is a GPT? A visual intro to transformers (3Blue1Brown)
seed-3b1b-gpt.hook: Beautiful animations that let you see how text becomes numbers and numbers become the next word.
seed-3b1b-gpt.summary:
Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown walks through what happens inside a GPT-style model, using his trademark animations. Text is split into small pieces called tokens, each token is turned into a long list of numbers (an embedding), and those lists flow through repeated layers, mainly attention blocks and simple feed-forward blocks, until the model produces a probability for every possible next token.

A memorable idea is that directions in this space of numbers can carry meaning, so related words end up near each other. He also explains how the final probabilities are produced and how a setting called temperature makes the output more predictable or more varied.

This is part of a deep learning series and is a step up from the Karpathy intro. Some maths appears, but you can follow the story without it. Watch for the big picture, not the formulas.
takeaways: Models do not see words; they see tokens, small chunks of text turned into lists of numbers.
Embeddings place tokens in a space where direction and distance can carry meaning.
Attention lets each token take information from the other tokens around it.
The output is a probability for every possible next token; temperature controls how adventurous the pick is.
The context window is how much text the model can consider at once.

steps.title: Watch without pausing for maths
steps.detail: Let the formulas wash over you. Track the journey: text, tokens, numbers, layers, next-word probabilities.

steps.title: Draw the pipeline
steps.detail: On paper, draw five boxes from left to right for that journey and label each in your own words.

steps.title: See tokens for real
steps.detail: Search for a free online tokenizer tool from a model provider and paste in a sentence. Notice how words get split.

steps.title: Play with temperature
steps.detail: If you have access to a model playground, ask the same question at low and high temperature and compare the answers.

exercise.title: Sketch the GPT pipeline
exercise.goal: Create a diagram you could use to explain a transformer to a friend.
instructions: Draw (on paper or in any drawing app) the path from a sentence to a predicted next word.
Include these labels: tokens, embeddings, attention, probabilities, temperature.
Write one plain sentence under each label explaining it.
Take a photo or screenshot and upload it.

quiz.q: What is a token?
options: A small chunk of text the model works with
quiz.explain: Text is split into tokens, which may be whole words or parts of words.

quiz.q: What does the attention mechanism let a token do?
options: Take in information from other tokens in the context
Skip the rest of the text
quiz.explain: Attention is how context flows between tokens.

quiz.q: A higher temperature makes the model's output...
quiz.explain: Temperature flattens the probabilities so less likely words get picked more often.

seed-karpathy-deep-dive.title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (Karpathy, watch in parts)
seed-karpathy-deep-dive.hook: The long version: how chat models are built, why they fail in odd ways, and how to use them well.
seed-karpathy-deep-dive.summary:
This is a three-and-a-half-hour lecture for a general audience that goes through the whole life of a chat model: collecting and filtering internet text, splitting it into tokens, training a neural network to predict the next token, then post-training it on human-written conversations so it acts as an assistant, and finally reinforcement learning, which is how newer 'thinking' models learn to reason step by step.

Along the way Karpathy explains practical quirks you will run into constantly: why models hallucinate, why they struggle with counting letters or spelling (tokens again), why they do better when allowed to work through a problem in steps, and why giving them information directly in the prompt beats relying on what they remember.

Do not try to watch it all today. Today, watch from the start through the section on post-training and hallucinations, the first hour or so. Save reinforcement learning and the 'thinking' models section for later in the week.
takeaways: A chat model is a pre-trained text predictor that has been taught, with example conversations, to behave like an assistant.
Models hallucinate because they imitate confident answers; tools like web search and clear context reduce this.
Putting the facts you need into the prompt works better than relying on the model's memory.
Models need room to think: asking for step-by-step work helps on tricky problems.
Odd failures such as miscounting letters often come from tokenization, not stupidity.

steps.title: Plan your viewing
steps.detail: Split the video into three sittings across the week. Today: up to and including post-training and hallucinations.

steps.title: Keep a 'quirks' list
steps.detail: Every time Karpathy mentions a weird failure mode, write it down with a one-line reason.

steps.title: Test a quirk
steps.detail: Ask an assistant to count a specific letter in a long word, then ask it to spell the word out letter by letter first and count again. Compare.

steps.title: Test context versus memory
steps.detail: Ask a question about a long text from memory, then paste the text in and ask again. Note the difference.

steps.title: Turn the quirks into prompting rules
steps.detail: Write three rules for yourself, such as 'give it the source text' or 'ask it to work step by step'.

exercise.title: My personal prompting rulebook, version 1
exercise.goal: Turn what you learned about model quirks into rules you will actually use with your coding agent.
instructions: List at least four quirks from the lecture in your own words.
For each, run a small test with an AI assistant and note what happened.
Write a rule that works around each quirk (for example: 'paste the error message, do not describe it').
Save the rulebook in your journal; you will add to it all program long.

quiz.q: Why do models often struggle to count letters in a word?
options: They see tokens, not individual letters
The internet has no spelling data
quiz.explain: Words are split into tokens, so individual letters are not directly visible.

quiz.q: What is a reliable way to reduce made-up facts?
options: Give the model the relevant information directly in the prompt
quiz.explain: Information in the context is used far more reliably than vague memory.

quiz.q: What does post-training on conversations change?
options: It gives the model internet access
It makes the base model behave like a helpful assistant
quiz.explain: Post-training shapes behaviour; most knowledge comes from pre-training.

quiz.q: Why ask a model to work step by step on a hard problem?
options: Each token has limited computation, so spreading work over more tokens helps
quiz.explain: Models need tokens to think; reasoning out loud gives them room.

seed-karpathy-software-3.title: Software Is Changing (Again): Karpathy on Software 3.0
seed-karpathy-software-3.hook: Why writing software in plain English is real programming, and where you fit in that shift.
seed-karpathy-software-3.summary:
In this keynote at Y Combinator's AI Startup School, Andrej Karpathy describes three eras of software. Software 1.0 is code people write by hand. Software 2.0 is neural networks whose behaviour is learned from data. Software 3.0 is programming large language models with prompts written in plain language.

He compares LLMs to utilities and to operating systems, describes their strange 'psychology' (superhuman at some things, oddly weak at others, and forgetful between sessions), and argues for 'partial autonomy' products: tools where a human stays in the loop, can quickly check the AI's work, and can slide how much control the AI gets. He also talks about vibe coding, building apps by talking to an AI, and how the hard part often moves to deployment and everything around the code.

This is a great end-of-foundation talk: it explains why the program teaches you to guide and verify an agent rather than type code from scratch.
takeaways: Prompts are a new kind of program: plain language can now drive software.
LLMs are powerful but uneven; they can be brilliant and make silly mistakes in the same session.
Good AI tools keep a human in the loop with a fast way to check and accept work.
Work in small, verifiable steps instead of asking for huge changes at once.
Getting code written is now easy; shipping it (deploys, accounts, payments) is often the hard part.

steps.title: Watch the full talk
steps.detail: Note his three eras of software and one example of each.

steps.title: Find your autonomy slider
steps.detail: Think about how much you let your coding agent do without asking. Write where you are on the slider today and why.

steps.title: Review two weeks of your own work
steps.detail: Look at what you built in the foundation weeks. Where did you verify carefully, and where did you just accept?

steps.title: Write your Software 3.0 statement
steps.detail: In three sentences: what you will build in the next phase and how you will keep the AI on a short leash.

exercise.title: Foundation retrospective
exercise.goal: Close the first two weeks with a clear picture of how you work with AI and what you will build next.
instructions: Write a short retrospective (200–300 words) on your first two weeks.
Include one moment where the agent saved you a lot of time and one where you had to catch its mistake.
Use at least two ideas from the talk (for example: partial autonomy, generation and verification, small steps).
End with which track you choose next (apps or video) and why.

quiz.q: In Karpathy's framing, what is Software 3.0?
options: Neural network weights trained on data
Software that runs only in the cloud
quiz.explain: 1.0 is hand-written code, 2.0 is learned weights, 3.0 is prompting LLMs.

quiz.q: What does a 'partial autonomy' product do?
options: Lets the AI act with no oversight
Keeps a human in the loop and lets them adjust how much the AI does
quiz.explain: The human verifies quickly and controls how much autonomy the AI gets.

quiz.q: Why work in small steps with an agent?
options: Small changes are faster to check, so mistakes get caught early
Agents cannot write more than ten lines
quiz.explain: Verification is the bottleneck; small diffs keep it fast.

suggestedDays.reason: Last day of foundation: step back and see the bigger picture before choosing a track.

seed-fireship-claude-37.title: Claude 3.7 goes hard for programmers (Fireship)
seed-fireship-claude-37.hook: A fast, funny snapshot of the release that brought Claude Code into the world, and a lesson in reading AI hype.
seed-fireship-claude-37.summary:
Fireship's quick video reacts to the launch of Claude 3.7 Sonnet and the first research preview of Claude Code, released at the same time in early 2025. In typical Fireship style it moves fast: what the new model claims, its option to think longer before answering, and a hands-on look at using the command-line agent.

Treat this as a time capsule. Models and tools have moved on since, so specific benchmarks and prices in the video are out of date. What still holds is the shape of working with an agent in the terminal and the healthy scepticism toward launch-day claims.

As you start the apps track, use it to remind yourself that the tools will keep changing. Your skill is in describing, checking and shipping, not in any single model version.
takeaways: Claude Code started as a terminal-based agent released alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet.
Extended thinking lets a model spend more effort on a hard problem before answering.
Launch-day benchmarks are marketing until you test the tool on your own work.
Model versions change quickly; durable skills are about process, not a specific release.

steps.title: Watch it once for fun
steps.detail: It is short. Enjoy the jokes, then go back for the substance.

steps.title: List the claims
steps.detail: Write down every concrete claim the video mentions about the model or the tool.

steps.title: Check what is current
steps.detail: Open the Claude Code docs and see which model it uses today and what has changed since.

steps.title: Run your own mini benchmark
steps.detail: Give your coding agent one small task from your app idea and judge the result yourself.

exercise.title: Hype check: my own test
exercise.goal: Form your own opinion of your coding agent based on evidence, not marketing.
instructions: Pick one small feature for the app you plan to build in this track (for example: a form that saves a note).
Ask Claude Code to build it in a new folder. Time how long it takes and count how many corrections you needed.
Write a short 'review' (100–200 words): what worked, what did not, and one thing you would ask differently next time.

quiz.q: What was released alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet?
options: A research preview of Claude Code
quiz.explain: Claude Code first appeared as a research preview at that launch.

quiz.q: What is the best way to judge a new AI tool?
options: Test it on your own real tasks
quiz.explain: Your own work is the benchmark that matters.

quiz.q: Why are some details in this video outdated now?
options: Models, prices and features change quickly
quiz.explain: AI tools move fast; focus on durable process skills.

seed-fireship-remotion.title: This video was made with code. But how? (Fireship on Remotion)
seed-fireship-remotion.hook: See how a whole video can be written as code, which is exactly the kind of code an AI agent can write for you.
seed-fireship-remotion.summary:
In this short video Fireship explains how he makes videos with Remotion, a tool that lets you build videos using React, the same technology many websites are made with. Each scene is a component, the current frame number drives what is on screen, and Remotion renders all the frames into a normal video file.

The big idea for this track: if a video is code, then you can describe a video to a coding agent and it can write it. Text that slides in, numbers that count up, charts that grow, captions that pop: all of this becomes a few lines that you can change, reuse and render again.

Do not worry about the React details yet. Watch for the mental model: a video is a function of time, and frames are just snapshots of that function.
takeaways: Remotion lets you build videos with React components instead of a timeline editor.
Everything on screen is calculated from the current frame number.
Because the video is code, it is easy to change, template and re-render.
This makes video a natural fit for AI coding agents: describe the motion, let the agent write it.

steps.title: Watch the video
steps.detail: Focus on the idea of frames and time, not the syntax.

steps.title: Think in frames
steps.detail: At 30 frames per second, how many frames is a 5-second clip? (150.) Write down three things you would animate in those 150 frames.

steps.title: Describe a 5-second clip
steps.detail: Write a short description: background colour, text, how it enters, how it leaves, timing in seconds.

steps.title: Ask your agent to scaffold it
steps.detail: In a new folder, ask Claude Code to create a Remotion project and build your clip. Let it run the setup commands with your permission.

steps.title: Preview it
steps.detail: Ask the agent how to open the Remotion preview in your browser and play your clip.

exercise.title: My first coded video clip
exercise.goal: Get a 5-second title animation running in the Remotion preview.
instructions: Write a description of a 5-second title card with your name or project name.
Ask Claude Code to set up a new Remotion project and build that clip.
Open the preview, play it, and ask for one change (colour, speed, or font size).
Take a screenshot of the preview showing your clip and upload it.

quiz.q: What does Remotion use to describe a video?
quiz.explain: Scenes are React components rendered frame by frame.

quiz.q: What usually decides what is on screen at any moment in a Remotion video?
quiz.explain: Animations are calculated from the frame.

quiz.q: Why is video-as-code a good fit for AI coding agents?
options: Agents cannot edit video files at all
You can describe the motion in words and the agent writes the code
It removes the need for any review
quiz.explain: Agents are good at writing code from clear descriptions, and you can still review the result.

suggestedDays.reason: Opening the video track: the core idea that video can be code.

seed-manim-3b1b-demo.title: How I animate 3Blue1Brown: a Manim demo with Ben Sparks
seed-manim-3b1b-demo.hook: Watch Grant Sanderson build a maths animation live and see how a creator actually works in code.
seed-manim-3b1b-demo.summary:
Grant Sanderson, creator of 3Blue1Brown, sits down with mathematician Ben Sparks and builds an animation from scratch with Manim, the Python library he created for his videos. The value here is not memorising the code but watching his workflow: he writes a little, runs it, looks, adjusts, and repeats, in very short loops.

One important detail: Grant uses his own version of Manim (often called ManimGL). Most beginners, and most tutorials, use Manim Community Edition, which is a separate, community-maintained fork. Code from this video may not run unchanged in the Community version. That is fine; you are here for the way of working.

The video is close to an hour long. Watch the first 20 minutes today to absorb the workflow, and come back to the rest when you are building your own scenes.
takeaways: Manim is a Python library for precise, programmatic animation, originally made for 3Blue1Brown.
Fast feedback loops matter more than perfect code: change, run, look, repeat.
There are two main versions: Grant's ManimGL and the separate Manim Community Edition.
Complex animations are built from many small, simple moves.

steps.title: Watch the first 20 minutes
steps.detail: Pay attention to how often Grant runs his code to look at the result.

steps.title: Note the building blocks
steps.detail: Write down the kinds of objects and moves he uses: shapes, text, equations, movements, transformations.

steps.title: Ask your agent which Manim to use
steps.detail: Ask Claude Code to explain the difference between ManimGL and Manim Community and which one is easier to install on your computer.

steps.title: Install and run a test scene
steps.detail: Ask the agent to install Manim Community and render a simple scene: a square that turns into a circle.

exercise.title: Square to circle
exercise.goal: Render your first Manim animation and practise the change-run-look loop.
instructions: With Claude Code, install Manim Community Edition (it will need Python and a few system tools; let the agent guide you).
Render a scene where a square transforms into a circle.
Make three small changes, one at a time, re-rendering each time: colour, speed, and an added text label.
Upload the final video file or a screenshot of its last frame.

quiz.q: Which language is Manim written in and used with?
quiz.explain: Manim scenes are Python classes.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between ManimGL and Manim Community?
options: One is for music, one for video
They are separate versions; code may not transfer directly between them
quiz.explain: Grant uses ManimGL; most tutorials use the Community fork.

quiz.q: What habit does the demo show that you should copy?
options: Write the whole scene before running anything
Run the code often and adjust in small steps
quiz.explain: Short feedback loops are how good animations get made.

seed-remotion-fundamentals.title: Remotion fundamentals: compositions, frames and animation
seed-remotion-fundamentals.hook: The official guide to the handful of ideas that every Remotion video is built from.
seed-remotion-fundamentals.summary:
This section of the Remotion docs explains the core concepts in a short series of pages. A composition is a video definition: a component plus its width, height, frames per second and duration. Inside it, a hook gives you the current frame, and you calculate what to show from that number. Helpers such as interpolate turn a frame range into a value range (for example, opacity going from 0 to 1 over the first 30 frames), and Sequence lets you place parts of the video at different times.

The docs also show how to preview your video in the Remotion Studio in your browser and how to render it to an MP4 file.

You do not need to read every page in the docs today. Read the fundamentals pages in order, and keep the rest of the docs as a reference you and your agent can come back to.
takeaways: A composition defines the video: component, size, fps and length in frames.
The current frame is the single source of truth for animation.
interpolate maps frames to values such as position, opacity or scale.
Sequence shifts parts of the video in time so you can build scenes.
You preview in the browser and render to a real video file when ready.

steps.title: Read the fundamentals pages in order
steps.detail: Stop after each page and say in one sentence what it taught.

steps.title: Open your Remotion project from the last lesson
steps.detail: Or ask Claude Code to create a fresh one if you do not have it.

steps.title: Find the concepts in your own code
steps.detail: Ask the agent to point out where the composition, the current frame and interpolate appear in your project.

steps.title: Add a second scene with Sequence
steps.detail: Ask it to add a second part that starts after your title card ends.

steps.title: Render to MP4
steps.detail: Ask how to render the composition to a video file and run it.

exercise.title: A two-scene, 10-second video
exercise.goal: Render a real MP4 that uses a composition, interpolate and Sequence.
instructions: Plan two scenes of about 5 seconds each: a title, then a short message or fact.
Build them with Claude Code in your Remotion project, using Sequence to place the second scene.
Make at least one property animate with interpolate (fade, slide or scale).
Render to MP4 and upload the file.

quiz.q: What does a composition define?
options: The component plus its size, fps and duration
quiz.explain: A composition is the full definition of one renderable video.

quiz.q: What is interpolate used for?
options: Mapping a range of frames to a range of values
quiz.explain: For example, frames 0–30 to opacity 0–1.

quiz.q: What does Sequence let you do?

quiz.explain: Sequence places children on the timeline.

quiz.explain: 10 seconds times 30 frames per second is 300 frames.

seed-manim-docs.title: Manim Community docs: installation and quickstart
seed-manim-docs.hook: The official home for Manim Community, with a quickstart that gets your first animation rendered.
seed-manim-docs.summary:
The Manim Community documentation covers installing Manim, a quickstart tutorial, deeper tutorials and guides, an example gallery and a full reference of every class. For a beginner the important parts are installation (Manim needs Python plus a few system tools, and LaTeX if you want to render maths formulas) and the quickstart, which builds a scene, renders it from the command line, and transforms one shape into another.

The example gallery is the best part to come back to: each example shows a short animation next to the code that made it, which makes it easy to point your agent at an example and ask for something similar.

Today, read the installation page for your operating system and the quickstart. Skim the example gallery to collect ideas. Leave the reference section for when you need a specific class.
takeaways: Manim scenes are Python classes with a construct method that lists what happens.
You render from the command line; low-quality preview renders are fast for iteration.
LaTeX is only needed if you want typeset maths formulas.
The example gallery pairs animations with code, which is perfect to show your agent.

steps.title: Read installation for your system
steps.detail: Note what is required. Ask Claude Code to check what you already have installed.

steps.title: Follow the quickstart with your agent
steps.detail: Ask Claude Code to walk through the quickstart steps with you, explaining each command.

steps.title: Browse the example gallery
steps.detail: Pick two examples you like and save their links.

steps.title: Remix one example
steps.detail: Give Claude Code the example link and ask for a version with your own text and colours.

exercise.title: Remix a gallery example
exercise.goal: Render a Manim animation adapted from the official gallery.
instructions: Pick one example from the Manim Community gallery.
Ask Claude Code to recreate it in your project, then change the text, colours and timing to fit a topic you care about.
Render it, first at low quality to iterate, then once at higher quality.
Upload the final video file.

quiz.q: Where do you describe what happens in a Manim scene?
options: In the construct method of a Scene class
quiz.explain: The construct method lists the animations in order.

quiz.q: Why render at low quality while working?
options: It renders much faster, so you can iterate quickly
It is required by the licence
quiz.explain: Fast previews keep your feedback loop short.

options: Only to render typeset maths formulas
quiz.explain: Plain text and shapes work without it.

seed-ffmpeg-docs.title: ffmpeg documentation: the core command-line tool
seed-ffmpeg-docs.hook: The Swiss army knife behind almost every video pipeline. Learn to read its manual so you can check what your agent writes.
seed-ffmpeg-docs.summary:
ffmpeg is a free command-line tool that converts, cuts, resizes, combines and re-encodes audio and video. This page is its main manual. It is long and technical, but its structure is logical: a synopsis of the command shape, a description of how ffmpeg reads inputs, processes streams and writes outputs, a section on stream selection (which audio or video tracks end up in the output), and then a long list of options.

The key mental model: options apply to the file that comes right after them. An input file follows -i, and the last path on the line is the output. In between you can set things like a start time, a duration, a video filter to resize, or a codec.

You will rarely write ffmpeg commands by hand; your agent will. Today, read the synopsis, the detailed description and the stream selection section, so you can understand and sanity-check the commands it proposes.
takeaways: An ffmpeg command is: options and inputs (after -i), then options and the output file.
Options apply to the next file on the command line, so order matters.
A file contains streams (video, audio, subtitles); you can choose which ones to keep.
Copying streams without re-encoding is fast and lossless; re-encoding lets you change format or quality.
Filters (such as scaling) transform frames between input and output.

steps.title: Read the synopsis and description
steps.detail: Draw the flow: input file, demuxer, decoder, filters, encoder, muxer, output file.

steps.title: Read stream selection
steps.detail: In your own words, write how ffmpeg decides which streams go into the output by default.

steps.title: Ask your agent for three commands
steps.detail: Ask Claude Code for commands to: trim a clip to its first 10 seconds, resize it to 720 pixels wide, and extract the audio as MP3.

steps.title: Explain each command back
steps.detail: Before running, explain every part of each command using the docs. Ask the agent only when you are stuck.

steps.title: Run them on your own clip
steps.detail: Use the MP4 you rendered earlier in the track.

exercise.title: Three ffmpeg transformations
exercise.goal: Produce three new files from one video, and understand every flag you used.
instructions: Take a video you made earlier in the track.
With your agent's help, create: a 10-second trim, a 720px-wide version, and an MP3 of the audio (or a silent-audio note if it has none).
Write each command with a one-line explanation of every option.
Paste the commands and explanations into your journal.

quiz.q: In an ffmpeg command, what marks an input file?
quiz.explain: Inputs follow -i; the last path is usually the output.

quiz.q: Why does the position of an option matter?
options: Options apply to the next file listed
Only the first option is used
quiz.explain: Placing an option before -i applies it to that input; before the output, to the output.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of copying streams instead of re-encoding?
options: It is fast and keeps the original quality
It shrinks the file a lot
quiz.explain: Stream copy repackages data without decoding it.

seed-cc-docs-overview.title: Claude Code overview: what it is and how to install it
seed-cc-docs-overview.hook: The official starting point: install Claude Code and run your first session today.
seed-cc-docs-overview.summary:
This page from the Claude Code documentation explains what the tool is and how to get it running. Claude Code is an agentic coding tool: it reads your project, edits files, runs commands and works with your development tools. You can use it in the terminal, inside code editors, in a desktop app and in the browser.

The page gives installation instructions and a short first-run walkthrough, plus links to the rest of the docs for when you need them. Installation steps change from time to time, so always follow the current version of this page rather than an old video or blog post.

Today's goal is simple: get Claude Code installed, sign in, and have one real conversation with it in a folder on your computer.
takeaways: Claude Code is an agent that works inside your project: reading, editing and running commands.
It runs in several places: terminal, editors, desktop app and browser.
Always follow the current docs for installation; steps change over time.
You start it inside a project folder, and that folder is what it works on.

steps.title: Read the overview page
steps.detail: Note which ways of using Claude Code are available and which one you will start with.

steps.title: Install it
steps.detail: Follow the install instructions for your operating system exactly. If a command fails, copy the full error message somewhere safe.

steps.title: Sign in
steps.detail: Complete the login flow the first time you run it.

steps.title: Start a first session
steps.detail: Create a new empty folder, open a terminal in it, start Claude Code and ask: 'What can you help me with in this folder?'

steps.title: Make one small file
steps.detail: Ask it to create a text file called hello.txt with a short note to yourself, then open the file to check.

exercise.goal: Have Claude Code installed and prove it can create a file on your computer.

In a new folder, start a session and ask it to create hello.txt containing today's date and one sentence about why you joined this program.

quiz.q: What does Claude Code work on when you start it?
options: The project folder you start it in
quiz.explain: It works in the folder where you launch it.

seed-cc-best-practices.title: Best practices for Claude Code
seed-cc-best-practices.hook: The official guide to getting consistently good results from your agent instead of lucky ones.
seed-cc-best-practices.summary:
This page collects the habits that make Claude Code reliable. The recurring themes: give the agent a way to verify its own work (run the app, run tests, compare with a screenshot), explore and plan before writing code, give specific context instead of vague requests, and set up your environment with a CLAUDE.md file so it knows your project's rules.

It also covers managing a session: correcting course early, clearing the conversation when you switch to an unrelated task so old context does not confuse it, and, for later, ways to automate and scale up such as running Claude in scripts or in parallel.

For now, focus on the first sections about verification, planning, specific prompts and CLAUDE.md. Skim the more advanced parts so you know they exist; you will come back to them in the Ship phase.
takeaways: The single biggest improvement is giving the agent a way to check its own work.
Explore, then plan, then code, then commit: separating these steps prevents wasted work.
Specific requests (which file, what behaviour, what it should look like) get better results than vague ones.
Keep CLAUDE.md short and useful: commands, conventions and gotchas for this project.
Clear the context between unrelated tasks so old details do not get in the way.

steps.title: Read the verification and planning sections
steps.detail: Write down how you could let the agent check your current project (for example, by opening the page in a browser and taking a screenshot).

steps.title: Rewrite a vague request
steps.detail: Take a past request like 'make it look better' and rewrite it with specifics: which page, which elements, what feeling, what to leave alone.

steps.title: Improve your CLAUDE.md
steps.detail: Ask Claude to review your project's CLAUDE.md against the page's advice and suggest a shorter, clearer version.

steps.title: Practise clearing context
steps.detail: When you finish a task, clear the conversation before starting an unrelated one, and notice whether answers stay focused.

exercise.title: Before and after: one feature, two ways
exercise.goal: See the difference good practices make on a real change to your project.
instructions: Pick one small improvement to your first web page.
Write a vague request and a specific one (with what to change, what to keep, and how to check it).
Use the specific version with Claude Code, asking it to plan first and to verify the result itself.
Write a short note comparing the two requests and what the agent did, plus your updated CLAUDE.md.

quiz.q: According to the guide, what is one of the most effective things you can do?
options: Give the agent a way to verify its work
Keep all tasks in one endless conversation
quiz.explain: Verification lets the agent catch and fix its own mistakes.

quiz.q: What is a good order for a non-trivial change?
quiz.explain: Understanding and planning first avoids building the wrong thing.

quiz.q: When should you clear the conversation context?
options: When switching to an unrelated task
quiz.explain: Stale context from another task can distract the agent.

quiz.q: What belongs in CLAUDE.md?
options: Short project rules, commands and conventions
quiz.explain: Keep it concise and relevant; never put secrets there.

seed-building-effective-agents.title: Building effective agents (Anthropic)
seed-building-effective-agents.hook: A clear, practical map of agent patterns, with the advice to start simple and add complexity only when it pays off.
seed-building-effective-agents.summary:
This article from Anthropic distils what they learned working with teams that build AI agents. It separates workflows, where code follows a fixed path and calls a model at certain steps, from agents, where the model decides its own steps and tool use as it goes. The building block for both is an 'augmented' model that can use retrieval, tools and memory.

It then walks through common workflow patterns: prompt chaining (one step feeds the next), routing (classify the input, send it to the right handler), parallelization (split work or ask several times and combine), orchestrator and workers (one model hands out subtasks), and evaluator and optimizer (one model drafts, another critiques). Finally it covers when a true agent makes sense and why clear tool design matters as much as prompt design.

The main advice is to start with the simplest thing that works, often a single well-written model call, and add steps only when they measurably help. Read the whole article; it is not long, and you will use these names for the rest of the program.
takeaways: Workflows follow predefined steps; agents choose their own steps and tools dynamically.
Start with the simplest solution, often one good prompt, and add complexity only when it helps.
Common patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer.
Tools need clear names, descriptions and examples; design them as carefully as prompts.
Agents trade cost and predictability for flexibility, so test them carefully.

steps.title: Read the article end to end
steps.detail: Make a one-line definition for each pattern as you go.

steps.title: Map patterns to your app
steps.detail: For the app you are building, write which pattern (if any) fits an AI feature you want.

steps.title: Start with one call
steps.detail: Ask Claude Code to add a single AI call to your app with a fixed prompt. Use a fallback text if no API key is configured.

steps.title: Add one pattern if it helps
steps.detail: If the single call is not good enough, ask the agent to turn it into a two-step chain or add an evaluator step, and compare results.

exercise.title: Pattern map for my app
exercise.goal: Decide, on paper first, the simplest AI design for one feature of your app.
instructions: Describe one AI-powered feature of your app in two sentences.
Draw the simplest design (likely one model call) and one more advanced pattern from the article.
Write when you would switch from the simple design to the advanced one, using a concrete signal (for example: answers are wrong more than one time in five).
Upload a photo or screenshot of the diagram with your notes.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a workflow and an agent in this article?
options: Workflows use no model at all
Workflows follow predefined paths; agents direct their own steps
quiz.explain: Control flow is fixed in workflows and model-driven in agents.

quiz.q: Which pattern sends each input to a specialised handler based on its type?
quiz.explain: Routing classifies first, then dispatches.

quiz.q: What does the article recommend as a starting point?
options: The simplest solution that works, then add complexity if needed
quiz.explain: Simplicity first; complexity only when it measurably helps.

quiz.q: In evaluator-optimizer, what do the two roles do?
options: One generates a response, the other critiques it for another round
quiz.explain: It is a draft-and-feedback loop.

seed-prompt-engineering.title: Prompt engineering overview (Claude docs)
seed-prompt-engineering.hook: The official starting point for writing prompts that get what you actually want.
seed-prompt-engineering.summary:
This page opens Anthropic's prompt engineering guide. Before any techniques, it asks you to have three things: a clear idea of what success looks like, a way to test against that, and a first draft prompt to improve. Prompting is treated as an iterative process, not magic words.

It then points to a set of techniques, roughly from most broadly useful to more specialised: being clear and direct, giving examples, letting the model think step by step, structuring prompts with tags, giving the model a role, chaining prompts together, and tips for long documents. Each technique has its own page.

Today, read the overview and the 'be clear and direct' page. If you have more time, read the pages on examples and on letting Claude think. Everything here applies to talking with your coding agent too.
takeaways: Define what a good answer looks like before you start writing prompts.
Prompting is iterative: draft, test, adjust.
Being clear and direct is the most widely useful technique.
Examples, step-by-step thinking and clear structure each improve results in different situations.

steps.title: Read the overview
steps.detail: List the techniques it links to in your own words.

steps.title: Read 'be clear and direct'
steps.detail: Note its advice about giving context: who the output is for, what it is for, and what done looks like.

steps.title: Pick a real task
steps.detail: Choose something you need this week, for example a short bio for your first web page.

steps.title: Write a weak and a strong prompt
steps.detail: Write a one-line prompt, then a clear one with context, audience, length and an example of the tone you want.

steps.title: Compare results
steps.detail: Run both in an AI assistant and note what changed.

exercise.title: Prompt makeover
exercise.goal: Show, with a real before and after, how a clear prompt changes the result.
instructions: Choose a real writing task you need (a bio, a page intro, a short message).
Write a quick one-line prompt and save the result.
Rewrite it using at least two techniques from the guide (for example: clear context and an example).
Paste both prompts and both results, plus two sentences on what improved.

quiz.q: What does the guide suggest having before you start prompt engineering?
options: Success criteria, a way to test, and a first draft
quiz.explain: You need to know what good looks like and how to check it.

quiz.q: Which technique is described as broadly useful for almost any task?
quiz.explain: Clear, direct instructions with context help everywhere.

quiz.q: Why include an example in your prompt?
options: It shows the model the format and tone you want
quiz.explain: Examples are a fast way to communicate style and structure.

seed-anthropic-courses.title: Anthropic's courses: API fundamentals and prompting, hands-on
seed-anthropic-courses.hook: Free, notebook-based courses that teach you to call Claude from code and write prompts that hold up.
seed-anthropic-courses.summary:
This GitHub repository holds Anthropic's educational courses, built as Jupyter notebooks you can run. The set includes an API fundamentals course (getting a key, sending messages, choosing models and parameters), an interactive prompt engineering tutorial, a course on real-world prompting, one on evaluating prompts, and one on tool use.

The repository suggests taking them in order, starting with the API fundamentals. That is the one that matters for your app this week: it shows how your code sends a message to Claude and reads the reply.

Running the notebooks needs an API key, which is a paid account. If you do not have one, you can still read the notebooks on GitHub, and your app should show an 'AI not configured' message with a sensible fallback instead of crashing. Today, work through the first parts of API fundamentals.
takeaways: Your app talks to Claude by sending a list of messages and receiving a reply.
Parameters such as the model and the maximum length of the reply shape what you get back.
API keys are secrets: keep them in environment variables, never in your code or repository.
Take the courses in order; API fundamentals comes first.

steps.detail: Note the list of courses and the suggested order.

steps.detail: Even without running anything, read the first notebooks to see how a request is built.

steps.title: Set up your key safely (optional)
steps.detail: If you have an API key, ask Claude Code to help you store it in an environment variable file that is ignored by git.

steps.detail: Ask Claude Code to add a single endpoint that sends a prompt to Claude and returns the reply, with a clear fallback message when no key is set.

quiz.explain: API fundamentals sets up everything the others build on.

quiz.q: Where should your API key live?
options: In an environment variable or secrets file that is not committed
quiz.explain: Keys in a repository can be found and abused.

quiz.q: What should your app do if no API key is configured?
options: Show a clear 'AI not configured' state and a fallback
Ask users for their own password
quiz.explain: A graceful fallback keeps the app usable and demoable.

seed-pro-git-en.title: Pro Git: chapters 1 and 2 for beginners
seed-pro-git-en.hook: The free, official Git book. Two chapters give you everything you need to save and share your work safely.
seed-pro-git-en.summary:
Pro Git by Scott Chacon and Ben Straub is the standard free book on Git, the tool that records the history of your project so you can go back in time and share your work. The whole book is long; you do not need all of it.

Chapter 1, Getting Started, explains what version control is, why Git works the way it does, and how to install and configure it. Chapter 2, Git Basics, covers the everyday commands: creating a repository, checking status, staging and committing changes, viewing history, undoing things, and working with remotes such as GitHub.

Today, read chapter 1 and the first sections of chapter 2 up to recording changes and viewing history. Your coding agent can run Git commands for you, but you need to understand what they do so you can tell whether your work is safe.
takeaways: Git saves snapshots of your project called commits, so you can always go back.
Files move through three states: modified, staged, committed.
git status is the command to run whenever you are unsure what is going on.
A remote (like GitHub) is a copy of your repository somewhere else, used for backup and sharing.

steps.title: Read chapter 1
steps.detail: Focus on what version control is and the three states of a file.

steps.title: Install and configure Git
steps.detail: Ask Claude Code to check whether Git is installed and help you set your name and email.

steps.title: Read chapter 2 up to viewing history
steps.detail: Try each command yourself in a practice folder as you read.

steps.title: Make three commits

steps.title: Read your history

quiz.q: What is a commit?
options: A saved snapshot of your project at a point in time
quiz.explain: Commits are the building blocks of your project's history.

quiz.q: Which are the three main states of a file in Git?
quiz.explain: Changes are made, staged for the next commit, then committed.

quiz.q: Which command shows what is changed and what is staged right now?
quiz.explain: git status is your 'where am I' command.

quiz.q: What is a remote?
options: A copy of the repository hosted somewhere else, like GitHub
quiz.explain: Remotes let you back up and share your work.

seed-github-hello-world.title: GitHub Hello World: repo, branch, pull request, merge
seed-github-hello-world.hook: A short official tutorial that walks you through the core GitHub workflow in your browser.
seed-github-hello-world.summary:
This GitHub Docs tutorial teaches the basic GitHub workflow without needing the command line. You create a repository, make a branch so you can work without touching the main version, commit a change on that branch, open a pull request to propose the change, and merge it.

This is the same workflow your coding agent will use when it pushes work and opens pull requests for you. Doing it once by hand in the browser makes those steps feel familiar instead of mysterious.

You need a free GitHub account. The tutorial takes well under an hour, so do all of it today.
takeaways: A repository holds your project and its history on GitHub.
A branch lets you work on a change without affecting the main version.
A pull request proposes your changes and shows exactly what is different.
Merging brings the approved changes into the main branch.

steps.title: Create a GitHub account
steps.detail: If you do not have one, sign up for a free account.

steps.title: Follow the tutorial step by step
steps.detail: Create the repository, a branch, a commit and a pull request exactly as described.

steps.title: Read your own pull request
steps.detail: Look at the changed lines view and make sure you understand what is shown.

steps.title: Merge it
steps.detail: Merge the pull request and check that the main branch now contains your change.

steps.title: Connect it to yesterday's work
steps.detail: Ask Claude Code to push the repository from your Git practice to a new GitHub repository.

exercise.title: My first merged pull request
exercise.goal: Complete the full branch-to-merge cycle and have a public repository to show for it.
instructions: Complete the Hello World tutorial in your GitHub account.
Make sure the README describes who you are and that you are in a 66-day program.

quiz.q: Why create a branch before making changes?
options: GitHub requires one branch per file
To work without affecting the main version
quiz.explain: Branches isolate work in progress.

quiz.q: What is a pull request?
options: A request to download a repository
A proposal to merge changes from one branch into another
quiz.explain: It shows the differences and lets them be reviewed and merged.

quiz.q: After merging, where do your changes live?
quiz.explain: Merging brings the changes into the target branch.

seed-cf-workers-start.title: Cloudflare Workers: deploy your first app from the command line
seed-cf-workers-start.hook: Put real code on the internet in minutes, with a public URL you can send to anyone.
seed-cf-workers-start.summary:
This Cloudflare guide shows how to create and deploy a Worker using the command line. A Worker is a small piece of code that runs on Cloudflare's network and answers web requests. The guide uses a setup command to create a new project, Wrangler (Cloudflare's command-line tool) to run it locally while you develop, and a deploy command to publish it to a free workers.dev address.

You need a free Cloudflare account and Node.js installed. Your coding agent can run every command for you; your job is to read what each command does, approve it, and check the result in the browser.

In the foundation phase, use it to deploy your first page. In the apps track, come back to it as the base for an app with its own API.
takeaways: A Worker is code that runs on Cloudflare's network and responds to web requests.
Wrangler is the command-line tool to create, run and deploy Workers.
Develop locally first, check it in the browser, then deploy.
Deploying gives you a public URL on workers.dev that anyone can open.

seed-mdn-getting-started.title: MDN: Getting started with web development
seed-mdn-getting-started.hook: The most trusted free guide to how websites are made, from the people who document the web.
seed-mdn-getting-started.summary:
MDN's Getting started module is a beginner course on building for the web. It helps you set up the tools you need, then walks you through creating your first website: planning what it should contain, writing the content with HTML, styling it with CSS, adding a little interactivity with JavaScript, and publishing it. It also introduces how the web works and the standards behind it.

You will have an AI agent writing much of your code, but you still need to know what HTML, CSS and JavaScript each do, so you can describe what you want and spot when something is off. MDN is where you check those facts.

Today, focus on the 'Your first website' path: what each of the three languages is responsible for and how a page comes together. Skip deep detail; you can always come back.
takeaways: HTML gives a page its structure and content.
CSS controls how it looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout.
JavaScript adds behaviour and interactivity.
Planning the content and look before building makes the result much better.
MDN is the reference to check when your agent's code or explanation seems off.

steps.title: Read the module overview
steps.detail: Note which articles make up the 'Your first website' path.

steps.title: Plan your page on paper
steps.detail: Decide the purpose, the content (a few headings and paragraphs), and two or three colours and fonts.

steps.title: Build the HTML with your agent
steps.detail: Ask Claude Code to create index.html with your planned content, and ask it to explain each tag it uses.

steps.title: Add CSS
steps.detail: Ask it to add a stylesheet that applies your colours and fonts. Change one value yourself and refresh.

steps.title: Add one small interaction
steps.detail: Ask for a tiny bit of JavaScript, such as a button that shows a hidden message.

exercise.title: My first web page, three layers
exercise.goal: Build a one-page site where you understand what the HTML, CSS and JavaScript each do.
instructions: Use your plan to build index.html, a CSS file and a small JavaScript file with Claude Code.
Add a comment in each file, in your own words, explaining what that file is responsible for.
Open it in a browser on both a laptop-sized and a phone-sized window and fix anything that looks broken.
Upload a screenshot of the finished page.

quiz.q: Which language gives a web page its structure and content?
quiz.explain: HTML marks up headings, paragraphs, images and links.

quiz.q: You want to change the page's colours and fonts. Which do you edit?
quiz.explain: CSS controls presentation.

quiz.q: What is JavaScript mainly used for on a web page?
quiz.explain: It responds to clicks, updates content and more.
